name: Rugged individualism
summary: Rugged individualism is the American doctrine Herbert Hoover named in 1928: progress comes from individual initiative and enterprise, equal opportunity and decentralized local self-government. Government acts as umpire, regulating monopoly and public utilities, but must stay out of running business, and hardship is met first by voluntary charity, mutual self-help and local government. Hoover insists it is not laissez faire and that it rejects both socialism and class domination.
scope: The doctrine as stated by Herbert Hoover, who used the phrase 'the American system of rugged individualism' in his 22 October 1928 speech (s2, s4) and elaborated it in American Individualism (1922, s3); the Yale teaching unit (s1) identifies the phrase with his view of government and business. It does not include Hoover's tariff, foreign, Prohibition or other policy beyond these texts, nor the later polemical use of the phrase for pure self-reliance or atomism, which Hoover's texts reject.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Hoover praises the founders for refusing hereditary dukedoms and says sons of the successful must not keep their fathers places by birth.

all-land-state-owned.rationale: Hoover opposes government ownership and operation of production as destroying self-government and initiative.

ban-cartels.rationale: Hoover endorses laws that maintain competition and destroy conspiracies to dominate markets, while defending big business as such.

central-planning.rationale: Hoover says government must keep out of production and distribution, calling this the deadline between American individualism and socialism, and doubts any body could plan the economy in advance.

class-collaboration.rationale: Hoover rejects class compartments and praises solidarity of all grades of employees in common service, and says groups at war with each other destroy individualism.

clerical-rule.rationale: Hoover says the world has been disillusioned of divine inspiration resting in a few and religious hierarchies.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Hoover says progress depends on competition among individuals and enterprises, the free-running mills of competition, though he pairs it with service and curbs on domination.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Hoover welcomes the spread of non-essentials as fertilizers of the finer flowers of life and a rising standard of living as the first public aim.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Hoover warns that organized groups dominating legislators would turn the country into a syndicalist nation and that government must stay out of business.

decide-locally.rationale: Hoover calls decentralized local responsibility the very base of the American system and says municipalities can succeed where federal government fails, though he accepts national regulation.

democracy-best.rationale: Hoover says democracy is the mechanism individualism invented and prospers through it, but also distrusts the crowd and mob emotion.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Hoover names the dictatorship of the proletariat among the catchwords that cloak hate and tyranny and calls Bolshevist party rule a tyranny.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Hoover rejects divine right and treats democracy as arising from individualism and government by the majority, though he values the divine in each person.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Hoover says the sons of the successful must not by birth continue to hold their fathers places of power.

economic-freedom.rationale: Hoover says economic freedom cannot be sacrificed if political freedom is to be preserved and that free speech does not live long after free industry and commerce die.

elective-rulers.rationale: Hoover rejects leadership by divine right or birth and holds that leaders must rise by ability, with democracy and government by the majority as the political mechanism.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Hoover says American individualism insists on the divine in each human being and secures equality before the law and political equality.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Hoover says it is clap-trap to pretend all men are equal in ability and that government can assure only liberty, justice and equality of opportunity.

farm-price-support.rationale: Hoover opposes government buying, selling and fixing farm prices as state socialism, yet welcomes farm cooperatives and agricultural credit, so the evidence points both ways.

human-decline-since-golden-age.rationale: Hoover holds that progress has steadily advanced and that the American system has brought unparalleled well-being.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Hoover says rewards for saving and skill must be kept as stimulus and that accumulated ownership selects leadership, so ownership income is defended.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Hoover celebrates roads, railways, cities, science, mass production and rising living standards as the fruit of American individualism.

limit-growth.rationale: Hoover says the only road to higher living standards is greater production and invention and that any reduction in the impulse to produce brings misery.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Hoover says progress depends on competition and that government running commercial business is slower and less able, but he also backs regulation of utilities and monopolies, so markets are favoured rather than left alone.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Hoover says the most potent force in society is its ideals and that right ideals are the great propelling force of progress.

moral-incentives.rationale: Hoover says self-interest cannot be abandoned as the motive of production and calls socialism a will-o-the-wisp for relying on altruism alone.

municipal-businesses-mixed-economy.rationale: Hoover says municipalities, being local and close to the people, can at times succeed in business where federal and state governments fail.

natural-rulers.rationale: Hoover rejects the idea that a special few are endowed to rule and wants leadership to come from free competition, yet says rare creative minds supply leadership, so the evidence points both ways.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: Hoover says American individualism is not capitalism, socialism or syndicalism, nor a cross between them, but its own system, and no middle ground.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Hoover says American individualism is no system of laissez faire and endorses regulation of utilities and laws against conspiracies, public works and economic justice.

no-business-privileges.rationale: Hoover says there must be no domination by any group or combination, business or political, and that business must keep out of government as government out of business.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Hoover makes service and responsibility to others part of individualism .

one-party-rule.rationale: Hoover says there must be no domination by any group in the Republic, business or political, and ties democracy to individualism.

party-controls-media.rationale: Hoover warns that bureaucracy in business forces government toward control of press and platform and that free speech cannot survive it.

person-over-state.rationale: Hoover holds that intelligence, character and the divine spark belong to individuals, not to groups or institutions, and that the aim of government is to secure each person liberty and opportunity.

production-for-use.rationale: Hoover says for generations self-interest cannot be abandoned as the motive of production and that socialism wrongly counts on altruism alone.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Hoover says rewards to saving and skill must be kept as the stimulus to production, and presents large capital as the aggregated savings of ordinary people, which does not fit a theory that profit is exploitation.

property-fundamental.rationale: Hoover says private property is not a fetich in America but an instrument that stimulates initiative, and cites uncompensated prohibition of the liquor trade, so property is not treated as very hard to override.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Hoover treats the right of property as a useful instrument for stimulating initiative and selecting leaders, not an end in itself.

public-ownership.rationale: Hoover opposes state ownership and operation of power, liquor and farm marketing as state socialism, and says nationalization of industry is the negation of American individualism.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Hoover grounds individualism partly in the divine spark of every person and says social progress needs the things of the spirit.

religion-illusion.rationale: Hoover bases individualism on the divine spark in each person and holds that spiritual forces are essential to social progress.

restore-past-order.rationale: Hoover rejects those who insist the future must repeat the past and wants a better, broader individualism moving forward.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: Hoover holds that economic freedom and political freedom stand or fall together and that the road of more government is the road to less liberty.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Hoover says that even if government business were more efficient his fundamental objection would remain, and wants every process tested against the basic premise of individualism.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Hoover celebrates civilization built by pioneers, science and industry as progress and sees no virtue in abandoning it.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Hoover rejects divine right of kings and any ruling class endowed with divine attributes.

separated-powers.rationale: Hoover says self-government requires decentralization and many checks and balances to safeguard liberty.

simple-living.rationale: Hoover says a high and increasing standard of living for all is the first aim of public life and a basis for civilization.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Hoover treats revolution as destructive and democracy as the political mechanism individualism built, to be improved from within.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Hoover rejects autocracy and holds government to law as umpire, with legal justice and authority applying to all.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Hoover says individualism is not merely an economic creed and that social and economic systems cannot advance unless inspired by things of the spirit.

state-as-business.rationale: Hoover argues commercial business needs concentrated responsibility while self-government needs decentralization and checks, so government cannot be run like a business.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Hoover describes government as an umpire keeping equality before the law, though he warns that where property controls the state, capital oppresses.

state-finances-worker-businesses.rationale: Hoover says government must keep out of production and distribution, and welcomes cooperatives only where they preserve individual initiative.

state-harmful.rationale: Hoover describes government as an umpire that maintains law and equality of opportunity, and so rejects the claim that the state is unnecessary.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Hoover grounds individualism in the divine spark in every person and spiritual forces in public life, and condemns Bolshevik tyranny.

strong-leader.rationale: Hoover holds self-government requires decentralization and many checks and balances to safeguard liberty, and distrusts concentrated authority.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Hoover treats free speech, free press and free assembly as the roots of liberalism and warns against government that controls them.

taxation-theft.rationale: Hoover treats taxes as a normal means of public finance and expects taxation to curb excessive fortunes, so he does not regard it as theft.

total-state.rationale: Hoover holds that bureaucracy in business leads to control of press and thought and that expanding government destroys liberty.

unions-good.rationale: Hoover lists labor unions among voluntary associations that train leaders and serve the public, but warns of domination by some labor leaders, so his view is favourable with reservations.

unions-run-economy.rationale: Hoover warns that groups dominating government would make a syndicalist nation and that government must keep out of production.

vanguard-party.rationale: Hoover condemns Bolshevist party rule and revolutionary leadership by a tyrannical few as the opposite of individual initiative.

wages-fall-to-bare-minimum.rationale: Hoover says production can be sustained only with fair division of the product and points to rising living standards for the whole people.

war-builds-character.rationale: Hoover says war is destruction and leaves the world poorer spiritually, and that blame belongs to war, not to constructive social systems.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Hoover opposes concentration of power, economic as well as political, as a reversion to autocracy and wants wealth spread through the lives of all.

workers-councils.rationale: Hoover condemns syndicalism and the dictatorship of the proletariat, and holds that the American political system rests on decentralized representative government.

notes: Sources are Hoover's own texts plus one teaching unit; no encyclopedia entry defining the phrase could be opened (Britannica, Etymonline blocked or offline). Themes searched in the local library: economy, government in business, relief, liberty, spiritual grounds, class and equality. Hoover's texts say nothing on culture, gender, religion in law, world affairs, ecology or technology policy, so those answers are null; Hoover's tariff, immigration and foreign policy were not borrowed because they are not tied to the doctrine by the defining sources. Hoover's 1931 unemployment relief speeches were read but not cited, because no defining source ties them to the phrase.
